lesson.title: Crowding Effects: How Density Itself Limits Populations
lesson.summary: Density-dependent factors, including competition, disease, and predation, intensify as a population becomes more crowded, creating a negative feedback loop that tends to push population size back toward carrying capacity.
lesson.body:
Some limiting factors do not just restrict a population, they restrict it more severely as the population gets more crowded. These are density-dependent factors, and they are the mechanism that actually makes the logistic growth curve bend the way it does. Intraspecific competition for food, water, or space intensifies as more individuals compete for the same fixed supply. Disease and parasites spread more easily when individuals live in closer contact, since higher density generally means higher contact rates. Predators can also key in on unusually abundant prey, a dynamic explored further in later chapters on interspecific interactions. In every one of these cases, the per capita cost of being alive in that population goes up as the population grows.

This is precisely what the (1 - N/K) term in the logistic equation represents mathematically. As N rises toward K, that term shrinks toward zero, dragging the growth rate down with it. Density dependence is the biological reality behind that piece of math: crowding itself becomes a brake on further growth, which is why populations governed by strong density dependence tend to level off near K rather than crashing past it or growing without limit.

One of the classic laboratory demonstrations of this comes from the ecologist G. F. Gause's experiments with Paramecium, a single celled protist, grown in test tubes with a fixed daily supply of food in the 1930s. When a small number of Paramecium were introduced, the population grew rapidly at first, much as the exponential model would predict. But as the population density increased, individuals increasingly competed for the same limited food, and metabolic waste products built up in the confined culture. The population's growth rate slowed in direct relation to how crowded the culture had become, and eventually leveled off at a stable population size, tracing out a curve very close to the logistic S shape. This is a clean illustration of density dependence in action, and it also nicely echoes the same food limited scenario used to work through the logistic equation itself.

Because density-dependent factors get stronger as a population grows and weaker as it shrinks, they act as a stabilizing negative feedback loop: a population above carrying capacity experiences intensified competition, disease, or predation that pulls it back down, while a population well below carrying capacity experiences comparatively little of that pressure and can grow relatively freely. That stabilizing tendency is what distinguishes density-dependent regulation from the factors covered next, which do not respond to density at all.
